passages.happening:
As his death draws near, David charges Solomon: “I am about to go the way of all the earth. So be strong and prove yourself a man” (verse 2). He tells him to walk in the LORD's ways and keep his statutes ‘as is written in the Law of Moses’ (verse 3), so that the LORD will keep his promise that David's descendants, if they walk faithfully, will never fail to have a man on the throne of Israel (verse 4).

Then David names three men. Joab killed Abner and Amasa, the commanders of Israel's and Judah's armies, ‘in peacetime to avenge the blood of war’ (verse 5). Solomon is to act wisely and ‘not let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace’ (verse 6). The sons of Barzillai, who stood by David when he fled from Absalom, are to eat at the king's table (verse 7). And Shimei, who cursed David on the road and to whom David swore he would not put him to the sword, Solomon is not to hold guiltless (verses 8-9).

‘Then David rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David’ (verse 10). He had reigned forty years, seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem (verse 11). ‘So Solomon sat on the throne of his father David, and his kingdom was firmly established’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The charge opens in the language of Deuteronomy and of the LORD's words to Joshua: be strong, keep the law, and you will prosper. Every later king in this book will be measured by that standard. David ties God's promise to his sons' faithfulness. In 2 Samuel 7 the promise stressed that God's loving devotion would never be taken away; here each king's share in it depends on walking faithfully. The Bible holds both: an unbreakable promise to the house of David, and real consequences for each king who turns away.

The second half settles old scores that David himself had left unsettled. Joab had murdered Abner (2 Samuel 3:27) and Amasa (2 Samuel 20:10) in peacetime, as though at war, and David had let it pass. Shimei, a man of Saul's clan from Benjamin, had cursed David as he fled from Absalom, and on his return David had sworn to him, “You shall not die” (2 Samuel 19:23). Barzillai, an old and wealthy man of Gilead, had provided for the king while he stayed at Mahanaim.

Wisdom comes up twice in David's instructions: ‘act according to your wisdom’ (verse 6) and ‘you are a wise man’ (verse 9). Here it seems to mean political shrewdness. In chapter 3 God will give Solomon a deeper kind, the discernment to judge his people well.

The word established frames the chapter, here at verse 12 and again at its end. It is the word of God's promise to David, that he would establish his son's kingdom.
passages.later: David's words to his son echo the LORD's words to Joshua: ‘Above all, be strong and very courageous. Be careful to observe all the law that My servant Moses commanded you’ (Joshua 1:7). Joshua had used David's phrase for his own death too: ‘today I am going the way of all the earth’ (Joshua 23:14).
passages.hard:
Why does David, at the end of his life, ask his son to deal with Joab and Shimei?

Readers are divided, and the text gives material for more than one answer. On one reading David is doing a king's duty he had failed to do. Joab had shed innocent blood in peacetime, and in Israel's thought innocent blood brought guilt that had to be answered. Shimei stood for the lasting resentment of Saul's supporters. On another reading the scene is troubling. David had sworn not to kill Shimei, and he hands the task to his son. The narrator records the words without comment.

Many interpreters hold both. The chapter shows the promise to David being kept, and it shows the mixed motives of the people through whom it was kept. It does not make David's last instructions a pattern for anyone. No one may take these verses as leave for revenge, and the New Testament says plainly, ‘Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath’ (Romans 12:19).
passages.asks: David's charge put faithfulness to God first and old scores last. Ask which of the two will come first in what you leave behind. And ask what wrong you have let stand that should have been dealt with justly while you could.

passages.happening:
Adonijah goes to Bathsheba, and she asks whether he comes in peace. He says that he does (verse 13). “You know that the kingship was mine,” he tells her, and all Israel expected him to reign, ‘but the kingship has turned to my brother, for it has come to him from the LORD’ (verse 15). He has one request: that she ask King Solomon to give him Abishag the Shunammite as his wife (verse 17). Bathsheba agrees to speak for him.

“The king stood up to greet her, bowed to her, and sat down on his throne. Then the king had a throne brought for his mother, who sat down at his right hand” (verse 19). She makes her small request, and Solomon promises not to refuse her. But when he hears it, he answers, “Why do you request Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Since he is my older brother, you might as well request the kingdom for him and for Abiathar the priest and for Joab son of Zeruiah!” (verse 22).

Solomon swears by the LORD that Adonijah has asked at the cost of his life. That same day he sends Benaiah, who puts Adonijah to death (verses 23-25).
passages.hearers:
Adonijah admits that the kingdom came to Solomon ‘from the LORD’ (verse 15), and then he asks for the young woman who had served David to the end. In that world, taking a former king's wife or concubine could be a claim to his place. Absalom had made such a claim openly (2 Samuel 16:21-22), and Abner's taking of Saul's concubine had been read the same way (2 Samuel 3:7). Solomon hears the request as an older brother's second bid for the throne, with Abiathar and Joab behind it.

The scene also shows the queen mother's place. Solomon rises, bows to his mother and sets a throne for her at his right hand, the place of highest honor. Later the book will record the name of each Judean king's mother, a sign of her public role.

And once more Abishag is spoken of, asked for and refused, and she does not speak.
passages.later: A psalm uses the seat at a king's right hand for the highest honor of all: “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet” (Psalm 110:1).
passages.hard:
Did Adonijah's request deserve death?

The text does not say what Adonijah intended. Solomon reads it as treason: the elder brother who had already proclaimed himself king, and who had been spared on condition (1:52), now asks for the woman who had served David to the end, which in that world could be a claim to the throne. Some readers accept Solomon's reading. Others think the request handed him a reason he was glad to have. The narrator records the oath and the order and does not say which.

In that world, kings who came to power often removed rivals and their households, and the Bible records it here without holding it up as right. What the reader also sees is that Abishag is asked for and refused, and never asked herself.
passages.asks: Adonijah said the kingdom had come to his brother from the LORD, and then reached for it anyway. Ask where you have said that God has settled something and gone on maneuvering. And ask who is being used as a means in a struggle you are part of.

passages.t: Abiathar sent home, and Joab at the altar
passages.happening:
Solomon tells Abiathar the priest to go back to his fields in Anathoth. He deserves death, the king says, but he carried the ark of the Lord GOD before David and shared all David's hardships (verse 26). ‘So Solomon banished Abiathar from the priesthood of the LORD and thus fulfilled the word that the LORD had spoken at Shiloh against the house of Eli’ (verse 27).

When the news reaches Joab, who had backed Adonijah though not Absalom, he flees to the tent of the LORD and takes hold of the horns of the altar (verse 28). Solomon sends Benaiah. Joab will not come out: “No, I will die here” (verse 30). Solomon gives the order to strike him down and bury him, ‘and so remove from me and from the house of my father the innocent blood that Joab shed’ (verse 31). Benaiah kills him, and he is buried at his own home in the wilderness (verse 34). Benaiah takes Joab's place over the army, and Zadok takes Abiathar's (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Abiathar was the last of the priestly family of Eli, who had served at Shiloh. He had escaped the killing of the priests at Nob and fled to David (1 Samuel 22:20), and he had been with him ever since. Solomon spares his life for that loyalty, but sends him home to Anathoth, a priestly town a few miles northeast of Jerusalem. From now on Zadok's family leads the priesthood, and the narrator ties the change to the word spoken against Eli's house generations before (1 Samuel 2:27-36). Centuries later the prophet Jeremiah came from a priestly family of Anathoth. Some scholars think he may have descended from Abiathar, but the text does not say so.

Joab grasps the horns of the altar, as Adonijah had. But the law said that a man who killed another on purpose was to be taken even from God's altar (Exodus 21:14), and Solomon uses that law. Joab had murdered Abner and Amasa in peacetime, and the king says that their blood will come back on Joab's own head, while David's house will have peace from the LORD.

The word blood runs through the chapter, seven times in Hebrew. In Israel's thought innocent blood created guilt that had to be answered, and the chapter uses the word to frame Solomon's acts as justice.
passages.later:
The man of God had told Eli, “I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest. He will do whatever is in My heart and mind” (1 Samuel 2:35). Readers have taken that priest to be Samuel, or Zadok and his line.

Jeremiah's book opens, ‘These are the words of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, one of the priests in Anathoth in the territory of Benjamin’ (Jeremiah 1:1).
passages.hard:
Is Solomon's securing of his throne justice, or ruthless politics?

Readers are divided, and the text gives material for both. On one reading each man condemned himself. Joab had murdered two commanders and backed a rival king; Adonijah's request was a bid for the throne; Shimei will break a sworn oath. The narrator frames the deaths in the language of law and justice, and ties Abiathar's removal to prophecy.

On another reading the chapter quietly shows the ruthlessness of court politics. David had sworn not to kill Shimei and passed the task to his son, and every charge serves Solomon's safety a little too neatly.

Many interpreters hold both together. The narrator in Kings often reports what kings did without approving every act, and his account of Solomon will turn critical. What is clear is that the throne is established, as God promised, by men whose motives were mixed. The chapter gives no one today a warrant to remove a rival, in a nation, a church or a family.
passages.asks: Joab ran to the altar after a lifetime of doing as he pleased. Ask whether there is a place you expect God to shelter you from what you have chosen. And ask how past loyalty, like Abiathar's, should weigh with you when someone you know has done wrong.

passages.happening:
Solomon summons Shimei and tells him to build a house in Jerusalem and stay there. ‘On the day you go out and cross the Kidron Valley, know for sure that you will die’, he says (verse 37). Shimei answers, “The sentence is fair” (verse 38), and he lives in Jerusalem a long time.

Three years later two of his slaves run away to Achish king of Gath. Shimei saddles his donkey, goes to Gath and brings them back (verses 39-40). Solomon summons him and asks why he has not kept his oath to the LORD (verses 42-43). The king reminds him of the evil he did to David, and says that David's throne will be secure before the LORD forever (verses 44-45). Then Benaiah strikes Shimei down. “Thus the kingdom was firmly established in the hand of Solomon” (verse 46).
passages.hearers:
Shimei belonged to Saul's clan and had cursed David as he fled from Absalom, then begged for mercy when David came back. He stood for the resentment of Saul's supporters in Benjamin. Solomon's terms keep him under the king's eye. The Kidron Valley ran along the east side of Jerusalem, and crossing it meant leaving the city.

Shimei agrees under oath. When he goes to Gath, a Philistine city whose king still had dealings with Israel, he goes for his runaway slaves, not to plot, but he has left the city against his oath. Solomon treats the trip as a broken oath to the LORD, and adds the old charge of cursing David.

The chapter ends as it began, with the kingdom firmly established. Between the two notes, every rival is gone.
passages.later:
Shimei's curses are told in 2 Samuel: ‘His name was Shimei son of Gera, and as he approached, he kept yelling out curses’ (2 Samuel 16:5).

The same Hebrew phrase for death made certain on a set day is used in Eden: ‘in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die’ (Genesis 2:17). In both places the death is certain from the day the line is crossed.
passages.asks: Shimei kept his word for three years and broke it over two runaway slaves. Ask what small errand might lead you across a line you promised not to cross. And ask how you hold together God's faithfulness to his promise and the hard ways it was kept here.
